strengths: Addresses important and well-motivated problem: training deep biologically plausible SNNs without explicit normalization
Mathematically principled E-I Init scheme with detailed derivations showing clear path to balance E-I inputs and gain control
Comprehensive ablation study (Table 2) convincingly demonstrates necessity of each component
Thorough technical analysis: gradient imbalance detection, emergent bimodal current distributions (Fig 3), and learned sparse edge-centric features (Fig 7)
Competitive performance surpassing other biologically-constrained baselines (92.12% CIFAR-10 ResNet-18 with 4 timesteps)
Clever adaptive stabilization mechanism avoiding limitations of fixed epsilon approaches
Clear presentation with well-organized methodology and comprehensive appendix
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental scope: only CIFAR-10/100, only image classification, only feedforward architectures, no neuromorphic datasets (N-MNIST, DVS), single input encoding scheme (direct encoding), fixed T=4 timesteps without ablation
Substantial performance gap with batch normalization (3.45% on CIFAR-10 ResNet-18), limiting practical applicability despite biological plausibility argument

Overstated biological plausibility: still uses non-biological backpropagation with STE and gradient-based learning rather than spike-timing-dependent plasticity; adaptive stabilization with sample-wise minima lacks neuroscientific grounding

Strong and potentially violated assumptions: Bernoulli spike model with independence assumption may not hold during training when correlated activity emerges; no analysis of assumption violation effects
Ad-hoc aspects: dynamic initialization from first batch lacks justification for sensitivity; fixed 4:1 E-I ratio not ablated; gradient scaling by 1/d lacks theoretical justification
Incomplete experimental rigor: no error bars/confidence intervals, no multiple runs reported, no sensitivity analysis for hyperparameters, no computational cost analysis
Limited novelty: E-I Init closely extends Cornford et al. (2021) from ANNs to SNNs; STE and gradient scaling are standard techniques; primary contribution is careful engineering

Analysis limitations: Figure 3 bimodal distributions lack quantitative characterization of when beneficial; Figure 7 feature visualization is qualitative and anecdotal; missing analysis of learned E-I dynamics across layers
Incomplete comparisons: missing comparisons with other BN alternatives in SNNs (layer norm, instance norm variants); DANN comparison uses ANN baseline not directly comparable
Reproducibility gaps: Algorithm 1 provided but implementation details unclear (exact p estimation, adaptive stabilization per-layer vs. per-sample ambiguity); code not yet available despite promise

strengths: Well-motivated approach addressing the important tension between computational performance and biological plausibility in SNNs
Principled technical design with E-I Init providing mathematically grounded initialization that achieves both E-I balance and gain control through exponential weight distributions
Comprehensive E-I Prop stabilization method cleverly addressing practical training challenges: adaptive divisive inhibition, STE for decoupling forward/backward passes, and gradient scaling
Thorough ablation study (Table 2) convincingly demonstrating necessity of each component, with informative failure modes
Emergent bimodal distributions (Figure 3) suggest the network learns a sophisticated mechanism beyond simple normalization, providing interesting biological insights
Strong experimental documentation with clear hyperparameters, reproducibility details, and commitment to code release
Proper incorporation of biological constraints (Dale's law, E-I circuits) into deep neural network training
weaknesses: Significant performance gap compared to BN-equipped SNNs (92.12% vs 95.57% on CIFAR-10 ResNet-18, ~3.5% absolute drop), limiting practical utility and inadequately addressed in the paper

Baseline comparisons conflate multiple variables (different timesteps T=3-64, architectures, experimental settings), making it difficult to isolate the contribution of the proposed method

Biological plausibility claims are overclaimed given remaining non-biological aspects: backpropagation through time for training, fixed E:I ratio (4:1) without justification, direct image encoding, and aggressive fast-spiking approximation

Limited biological insights—paper claims to provide 'a computational platform for exploring lateral inhibition functions' but performs no such exploration; bimodal distributions shown but not mechanistically explained

Incomplete method analysis: architecture-dependent performance variations (ResNet > VGG) not explored; failure cases not discussed; limited investigation of what networks actually learn about lateral inhibition
Heavy notation with superscripts/subscripts reduces clarity; important details scattered across main text and appendix

Rigorous mathematical framework with detailed derivations: E-I Init is principled and well-justified with comprehensive appendices (D.2-D.4)
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple datasets (CIFAR-10/100, TinyImageNet, CIFAR10-DVS, DVS-Gesture) and architectures (VGG-8/11/16/19, ResNet-18)
Thorough ablation study (Table 2) convincingly demonstrates necessity of each component

Competitive results: 92.05% on CIFAR-10 with ResNet-18, exceeding prior E-I constrained methods

weaknesses: Significant computational overhead (2.3-2.5× training time, 1.1-1.6× memory) that substantially limits practical applicability, and insufficient discussion of when this trade-off is worthwhile

Critical technical inconsistency: forward pass uses nonlinear max operation for inhibitory spikes (Eq. 7), but gradient derivations assume linear approximation s_I[t] ≈ W_IE s_E[t]. This mismatch requires explicit justification

E-I Prop components lack theoretical rigor: adaptive stabilization is heuristic, STE correctness not formally justified, and gradient scaling factor 1/d lacks theoretical necessity (only empirical justification)
Overclaimed biological realism: fast-spiking approximation introduces simplifications, E-I ratio fixed at 4:1 without ablation, and biological plausibility claims should be more carefully qualified
Limited novelty: E-I Init closely follows Cornford et al. (2021), primarily extending it to temporal SNNs; main contribution is integration of existing techniques rather than fundamental innovation
Hardware deployment still challenging: division operations and adaptive stabilization remain difficult on digital neuromorphic hardware, undermining key motivation for avoiding normalization
